units.title: Note names, half steps and whole steps
units.summary: Calling notes by letters / the smallest distance between notes

cards.title: Notes are named with letters
text: In jazz, do re mi fa sol la ti are called C D E F G A B. Chord names use these letters too.
Do = C, Re = D, Mi = E, Fa = F, Sol = G, La = A, Ti = B.

cards.title: Half steps and whole steps
text: On a piano, the distance from one key to the very next key, black keys included, is a half step. Two half steps make a whole step.
There is no black key between E and F or between B and C, so those two pairs of white keys are a half step apart.

cards.title: ♯ (sharp) and ♭ (flat)
text: ♯ raises a note a half step, and ♭ lowers it a half step.
C♯ and D♭ are the same pitch, but we pick the name that fits the situation (enharmonic notes).

cards.title: On saxophone, the written note and the sounding note differ
text: The saxophone is a transposing instrument. The note written on the page (written pitch) is different from the note you hear (concert pitch).
On alto, a written C sounds as E♭. On tenor, a written C sounds as B♭ (an octave lower as well).
The Concert / Alto / Tenor switch at the top changes every note name, staff and chord name in this app to that instrument's written pitch. The sound is always concert pitch.
The note in the example below is currently shown as "{n:C4}". In concert pitch it is C.

units.title: Intervals (distance between notes)
units.summary: 3rds, 5ths and 7ths. Chords are built from intervals

cards.title: Intervals are counted in numbers
text: The distance between two notes is called an interval, and it is counted with numbers. The same note is a 1st (unison); the next letter is a 2nd.
Counting three letters, {n:C4}, {n:D4}, {n:E4}, makes {n:C4} to {n:E4} a 3rd. {n:C4} to {n:G4} is a 5th.

cards.title: Major 3rd and minor 3rd
text: A 3rd that spans 4 half steps is a major 3rd; one that spans 3 half steps is a minor 3rd.
{n:C4}→{n:E4} is a major 3rd, {n:C4}→{n:Eb4} is a minor 3rd. This difference makes a chord bright or dark.

cards.title: Perfect 5th
text: 7 half steps make a perfect 5th: {n:C4}→{n:G4}. It blends well and sounds stable, so it forms the base of a chord.

cards.title: Major 7th and minor 7th
text: 11 half steps make a major 7th; 10 half steps make a minor 7th.
{n:C4}→{n:B4} is a major 7th, {n:C4}→{n:Bb4} is a minor 7th. Jazz chords almost always include one of these 7ths.

units.title: The major scale
units.summary: Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half. Keys and degrees

cards.title: Whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half
text: The do-re-mi-fa-sol-la-ti-do sequence is the major scale. Its steps go "whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half".
Start on {n:C4} and you get the {n:C4} major scale. The starting note is called the key.

cards.title: The same pattern in every key
text: When you start on another note, add ♯ or ♭ so the steps still go "W W H W W W H".
In the key of {n:F4} the 4th note is {n:Bb4}; in the key of {n:G4} the 7th note is {n:F#5}.

cards.title: Calling notes by number (degrees)
text: Scale notes are called by number: 1st, 2nd, and so on (scale degrees). In jazz you think of chords and phrases as "which note of the key".
In the key of {n:C4}, the 1st is {n:C4}, the 3rd is {n:E4} and the 5th is {n:G4}.

units.title: Triads (major and minor)
units.summary: Three-note chords. The 3rd decides bright or dark

cards.title: Stack three notes, skipping one each time
text: Stack three scale notes, skipping every other note, and you get a triad. It is made of the root (the base note of the chord), the 3rd and the 5th.
Stack {n:C4}, {n:E4} and {n:G4} and you get the chord {c:C}.

cards.title: Major and minor differ only in the 3rd
text: A major 3rd above the root makes it major (bright); a minor 3rd makes it minor (dark).
{c:C} = {n:C4}, {n:E4}, {n:G4}; {c:Cm} = {n:C4}, {n:Eb4}, {n:G4}. Only the middle note is different.

cards.title: Reading chord names
text: A letter alone means major; a lowercase m after it means minor.

units.title: Four kinds of 7th chords
units.summary: maj7, 7, m7, m7♭5. Jazz is built on four-note chords

cards.title: Add a fourth note, the 7th
text: Add a 7th on top of a triad and you get a 7th chord. In jazz, these four-note chords are the norm.
Combining the 3rd (major or minor), the 5th (perfect or diminished) and the 7th (major or minor), these four kinds are the most common.

cards.title: maj7 (major seventh)
text: Major triad + major 7th. {c:Cmaj7} = {n:C4}, {n:E4}, {n:G4}, {n:B4}.
Calm and settled. Often used where the music "arrives home", like the end of a tune.

cards.title: 7 (dominant seventh)
text: Major triad + minor 7th. {c:C7} = {n:C4}, {n:E4}, {n:G4}, {n:Bb4}.
Tense, and it wants to move to the next chord. In the blues, this chord is the star.

cards.title: m7 (minor seventh)
text: Minor triad + minor 7th. {c:Cm7} = {n:C4}, {n:Eb4}, {n:G4}, {n:Bb4}.
Soft, with a slight shadow.

cards.title: m7♭5 (minor seven flat five)
text: An m7 with the 5th lowered a half step (a diminished 5th). {c:Cm7b5} = {n:C4}, {n:Eb4}, {n:Gb4}, {n:Bb4}.
Dark and unstable. Also called half-diminished, and sometimes written "ø".

units.title: Reading chord tones
units.summary: From a chord name to its root, 3rd, 5th and 7th

cards.title: Stack intervals from the root
text: When you see a chord name, stack the 3rd, 5th and 7th on the root to find the notes.
For {c:Dm7}: from the root {n:D4}, a minor 3rd {n:F4}, a perfect 5th {n:A4} and a minor 7th {n:C5}.

cards.title: The same with a flat root
text: For {c:Bb7}: from the root {n:Bb3}, a major 3rd {n:D4}, a perfect 5th {n:F4} and a minor 7th {n:Ab4}.
A ♭ or ♯ on the root doesn't change how you count.

cards.title: Learn in written pitch, play right away
text: When you play saxophone, learning chord names and notes in written pitch connects straight to your fingers.
Set the switch at the top to your instrument before you practice.

units.title: Diatonic chords
units.summary: Seven chords built only from scale notes, and Roman numerals

cards.title: 7th chords from scale notes only
text: Take each scale note as a root and stack four scale notes, skipping every other one. You get seven 7th chords, called diatonic chords.

cards.title: Naming them with Roman numerals
text: Roman numerals show which scale note the chord is built on.
Imaj7, IIm7, IIIm7, IVmaj7, V7, VIm7, VIIm7♭5. This order of chord types is the same in every key.

cards.title: In another key
text: In the key of {n:F4}: {c:Fmaj7}, {c:Gm7}, {c:Am7}, {c:Bbmaj7}, {c:C7}, {c:Dm7}, {c:Em7b5}.
Learn them as Roman numerals and you can apply them to any key at once.

units.title: The II–V–I
units.summary: IIm7 → V7 → Imaj7. The most common progression in jazz

cards.title: The most common progression in jazz
text: The motion IIm7 → V7 → Imaj7 is called the II–V–I (2-5-1). Many standards are made of chains of this progression.
In the key of {n:C4}: {c:Dm7} → {c:G7} → {c:Cmaj7}.

cards.title: Tension, then release
text: V7 is a tense chord, and moving to Imaj7 feels like landing. This is called resolution.
IIm7 is the run-up to V7.

cards.title: In any key
text: In {n:Bb3}: {c:Cm7} → {c:F7} → {c:Bbmaj7}. In {n:F4}: {c:Gm7} → {c:C7} → {c:Fmaj7}.

cards.title: Play it to check
text: Play phrases over this progression. Keep in mind which note is which degree of which chord as you play.

units.title: Guide tones
units.summary: Connect 3rds and 7ths and the changes become a smooth melody

cards.title: The 3rd and 7th are the face of the chord
text: The 3rd and 7th decide a chord's character (major or minor, maj7 or 7). These two notes are called guide tones.
The bass plays the root, and leaving out the 5th barely changes the sound.

cards.title: The 7th drops a half step to the next 3rd
text: The 7th of {c:Dm7}, {n:C5}, drops a half step to the 3rd of {c:G7}, {n:B4}. The 7th of {c:G7}, {n:F4}, drops a half step to the 3rd of {c:Cmaj7}, {n:E4}.
This half-step motion is the secret of smooth changes.

cards.title: The 3rd stays and becomes the next 7th
text: The 3rd of {c:Dm7}, {n:F4}, doesn't move and becomes the 7th of {c:G7}.
Connect the guide tones and one note stays while the other drops a half step. The chords change with hardly any movement.

cards.title: Try playing only guide tones
text: A first step in improvising is to connect each chord's guide tones with long notes.
Play them along with the accompaniment and you already have a melody that outlines the changes.

units.title: Tensions (9th, 11th, 13th)
units.summary: Notes stacked above the 7th that add color to a chord

cards.title: Keep stacking 3rds above the 7th
text: Keep stacking 3rds above the 7th and you get the 9th, 11th and 13th. These are called tensions.
The 9th, 11th and 13th are the same note names as the 2nd, 4th and 6th, counted an octave higher. The 9th of {c:Cmaj7} is {n:D5}.

cards.title: Tensions that fit each chord type
text: {c:Cmaj7} takes the 9th, ♯11th and 13th; {c:Dm7} takes the 9th and 11th.
{c:G7} is the most flexible: besides the 9th and 13th, it can use half-step-shifted notes like the ♭9th and ♯9th.
The examples leave out the root and add tensions (the bass plays the root).
In the example, {n:E5} is the 9th of {c:Dm7}; {n:A4} is the 9th and {n:E5} the 13th of {c:G7}; and {n:D5} is the 9th of {c:Cmaj7}.

cards.title: Clashing notes (avoid notes)
text: Hold the 11th, {n:F5}, over {c:Cmaj7} and it rubs a half step against the 3rd, {n:E4}, making a muddy sound. Notes like this are called avoid notes.
On major-type chords, raise the 11th a half step to {n:F#5} (the ♯11th) for a clear sound.

units.title: The minor II–V–I
units.summary: IIm7♭5 → V7(♭9) → Im7. The classic bittersweet progression

cards.title: The II–V–I in a minor key
text: In a minor key, the progression is IIm7♭5 → V7(♭9) → Im7.
In {n:C4} minor: {c:Dm7b5} → {c:G7b9} → {c:Cm7}. It sounds dark and a little bittersweet.

cards.title: The difference from major is the flatted note
text: Compared with {c:Dm7} in major, {c:Dm7b5} has its 5th lowered a half step to {n:Ab4}.
{c:G7b9} contains the same {n:Ab4} as its ♭9th. This note carries the minor feeling.
The example sets {c:Dm7} beside {c:Dm7b5}, then {c:G7} beside {c:G7b9}. In each pair, the chord with {n:Ab4} sounds darker.

cards.title: Connect with guide tones
text: The 7th of {c:Dm7b5}, {n:C5}, drops a half step to the 3rd of {c:G7b9}, {n:B4}.
The 7th of {c:G7b9}, {n:F4}, drops a whole step to the 3rd of {c:Cm7}, {n:Eb4}. Just as in major, the voices move a little at a time.

units.title: Secondary dominants
units.summary: Any chord in the key can have a 7 chord leading into it

cards.title: Any chord can get its own dominant
text: Like {c:G7} → {c:Cmaj7}, a 7 chord is strongly pulled toward the chord a perfect 5th below.
Put a 7 chord a perfect 5th above any other chord in the key and you get the same pull. This is called a secondary dominant.
In the example, {c:A7} is the 7 chord a perfect fifth above {c:Dm7} and pulls toward it; then the usual {c:G7} → {c:Cmaj7} follows.

cards.title: Secondary dominants in C
text: To {c:Dm7}: {c:A7}. To {c:Em7}: {c:B7}. To {c:Fmaj7}: {c:C7}. To {c:G7}: {c:D7}. To {c:Am7}: {c:E7}.
A note outside the key ({n:G#4} in {c:E7}) shines a light on where the music is heading.

cards.title: A common pattern: I → VI7 → IIm7 → V7
text: Just changing the diatonic {c:Am7} to {c:A7} strengthens the pull toward the next chord, {c:Dm7}.

units.title: Tritone substitution
units.summary: Replace V7 with the 7 chord 6 half steps away

cards.title: The tritone
text: An interval of three whole steps, or 6 half steps, is called a tritone. It is the same distance as a diminished 5th.
The 3rd of {c:G7}, {n:B3}, and its 7th, {n:F4}, are exactly a tritone apart. This restless sound is where the urge to resolve comes from.

cards.title: A partner with the same tritone
text: The 3rd of {c:Db7} is {n:F4} and its 7th is {n:Cb5} (the same pitch as {n:B4}). It has the same tritone as {c:G7}, with the 3rd and 7th swapped.
So {c:Db7} can stand in for {c:G7}. This is called a tritone substitution (tritone sub).

cards.title: The bass walks down in half steps
text: {c:Dm7} → {c:Db7} → {c:Cmaj7}. The bass goes {n:D4}→{n:Db4}→{n:C4} in half steps and resolves smoothly.

units.title: The blues progression
units.summary: One chorus in 12 bars. The form jazz musicians play most

cards.title: The 12-bar blues
text: A blues goes around once every 12 bars. The basic version uses only three chords: I7, IV7 and V7. All of them being 7 chords is what makes it sound like the blues.
In the key of {n:F4}: {c:F7}, {c:Bb7}, {c:C7}.

cards.title: The jazz blues progression
text: {c:D7} in bar 8 is a secondary dominant heading to {c:Gm7}. Bars 9–10 are a II–V.

The example shows the four chords of bars 11–12 ({c:F7} → {c:D7} → {c:Gm7} → {c:C7}). They move I7 → VI7 → IIm7 → V7, and the last {c:C7} leads back to {c:F7} in bar 1. A passage like this that takes you back to the top is called a turnaround.

cards.title: Blue notes
text: In the blues, you play the minor 3rd ({n:Ab4} over {c:F7}) even over a major chord. This is called a blue note.
Slide up a half step from {n:Ab4} to {n:A4} for a classic bluesy inflection.

units.title: Chords and scales
units.summary: Choosing which scale (mode) to play on each chord

cards.title: Choosing a scale from the chord
text: When improvising, you pick a scale that fills the gaps between the chord tones.
For {c:Dm7} in the key of {n:C4}, play the notes of the C major scale in order starting on {n:D4}. This is called Dorian.

cards.title: Four basic scales
text: Imaj7 takes Ionian (the major scale itself), IIm7 takes Dorian, V7 takes Mixolydian and VIIm7♭5 takes Locrian.
In the key of {n:C4}: {c:Cmaj7}, {c:Dm7}, {c:G7}, {c:Bm7b5}. All of them use only notes of the key.

cards.title: The colors of Dorian and Mixolydian
text: Dorian is minor, yet its 6th is bright ({n:B4} over {c:Dm7}).
Mixolydian is major, yet its 7th is low ({n:F5} over {c:G7}). That one note gives each its color.

units.title: Diminished chords
units.summary: dim7 stacks minor 3rds. It is really a 7(♭9) without its root

cards.title: Stack four minor 3rds
text: A dim7 (diminished seventh) stacks four notes a minor 3rd apart. {c:Bdim7} is {n:B3}, {n:D4}, {n:F4}, {n:Ab4}.
Every neighboring pair is the same distance apart, so it sounds tense, as if hanging in the air.

cards.title: Really a 7(♭9) without its root
text: Take the root {n:G3} out of {c:G7b9} and the remaining {n:B3}, {n:D4}, {n:F4}, {n:Ab4} are the same notes as {c:Bdim7}.
That is why a dim7 can stand in for a dominant and pull toward the next chord.

cards.title: Passing diminished
text: {c:Cmaj7} → {c:C#dim7} → {c:Dm7}. The bass climbs {n:C4}→{n:C#4}→{n:D4} by half steps, smoothly linking the chords.
{c:C#dim7} is also {c:A7b9}, which leads to {c:Dm7}, with the root left out.

units.title: Subdominant minor and the backdoor
units.summary: Borrowing chords from the minor key on the same tonic

cards.title: Borrowing from the minor key
text: A tune in {n:C4} sometimes borrows chords from the minor key that also has {n:C4} as its tonic.
The most often borrowed is {c:Fm7} (IVm7). {c:Fmaj7} → {c:Fm7} → {c:Cmaj7} sounds bittersweet and warm.

cards.title: The subdominant minor family
text: Besides IVm7, {c:Bb7} (♭VII7) and {c:Abmaj7} (♭VImaj7) belong to the same family.
All of them contain {n:Ab4}, which is not in the key of {n:C4}. This note is the color of subdominant minor.

cards.title: The backdoor II–V
text: {c:Fm7} → {c:Bb7} → {c:Cmaj7} is called the backdoor, because it comes home through the back door.
Instead of {c:G7}, it resolves to {c:Cmaj7} from {c:Bb7}, a whole step below.

units.title: Chains of II–Vs
units.summary: Pair every 7 chord with a IIm7 and link them together

cards.title: The related II
text: Before a secondary dominant you can put its paired IIm7. This is called the related II.
{c:A7} heads to {c:Dm7}, so its partner is {c:Em7}, the IIm7 seen from {n:D4}: {c:Em7} → {c:A7} → {c:Dm7}.

cards.title: Chains of II–Vs
text: m7 → 7 pairs keep falling by perfect 5ths. You meet this shape all the time in standards.

cards.title: Chains with tritone subs
text: Swap the 7 chords for tritone subs: {c:Em7} → {c:Eb7} → {c:Dm7} → {c:Db7} → {c:Cmaj7}.
The bass walks down in half steps, making a smooth chain.

units.title: Altered tensions
units.summary: Half-step-shifted tensions that only 7 chords can use

cards.title: Altered notes just for dominants
text: On a 7 chord you can use the 9th and 13th shifted by a half step, ♭9th, ♯9th, ♭13th, and the 11th raised to ♯11th. These are called altered tensions.
The example puts the ♭13th {n:Ab4} and the ♭9th {n:Db5} on top of the 7th {n:Bb3} and 3rd {n:E4} of {c:C7} (the root is left to the bass).

cards.title: Choose by where it resolves
text: In {c:G7} → {c:Cm7}, resolving to minor, the ♭9th and ♭13th ({n:Ab4}, {n:Eb5}) match the key and sound natural.
In {c:G7} → {c:Cmaj7}, resolving to major, the 9th and 13th ({n:A4}, {n:E5}) sound natural. Using the ♭9th on purpose creates strong tension.
The example shows the minor case: the ♭9th {n:Ab4} and ♭13th {n:Eb5} over the 3rd {n:B3} and 7th {n:F4} of {c:G7}, moving to {c:Cm7}.

cards.title: Compare the 9th and ♭9th by ear
text: {c:G9} sounds bright and open; {c:G7b9} sounds dark and sharp. The only difference is one half step: {n:A4} or {n:Ab4}.

units.title: Coltrane changes
units.summary: Rapid key changes by major 3rds

cards.title: Dividing the octave into three major 3rds
text: Stack three major 3rds and you land exactly an octave up: {n:C4}→{n:E4}→{n:G#4}→{n:C5}.
John Coltrane put a key on each of these three points and wrote progressions that change key quickly, one after another.

cards.title: Coltrane changes
text: {c:Cmaj7} → {c:Eb7} → {c:Abmaj7} → {c:B7} → {c:Emaj7}.
Three keys falling by major 3rds, {n:C4}, {n:Ab3}, {n:E4}, each reached through its own V7. The opening of "Giant Steps" uses this shape starting in the key of {n:B3}.

cards.title: Warm up with II–Vs
text: Jumping straight in is hard, so start by linking familiar II–V–Is shifted by a major 3rd.
{c:Dm7} → {c:G7} → {c:Cmaj7} → {c:Bbm7} → {c:Eb7} → {c:Abmaj7}.

units.title: sus4 chords
units.summary: A 4th instead of the 3rd. A sound that delays resolution

cards.title: Suspending the 3rd up to the 4th
text: A sus4 chord has a 4th in place of the 3rd. {c:G7sus4} is {n:G3}, {n:C4}, {n:D4}, {n:F4}.
Without the 3rd that decides major or minor, it sounds suspended, neither one nor the other.

cards.title: The 4th falls to the 3rd and resolves
text: {c:G7sus4} → {c:G7}. When the 4th, {n:C4}, drops a half step to the 3rd, {n:B3}, it turns back into an ordinary dominant.
In jazz, it is common to leave it unresolved and let the sus4 ring for a long time.

cards.title: II and V at once
text: Play the notes of {c:Dm7} over a {n:G3} in the bass and it sounds close to {c:G7sus4}.
It layers IIm7 over V7, so one chord can do the work of a whole II–V.
Compare them in the example: {c:Dm7} ({n:D4}, {n:F4}, {n:A4}, {n:C5}) and {c:G7sus4} ({n:G3}, {n:C4}, {n:D4}, {n:F4}) share three notes, {n:C4}, {n:D4} and {n:F4}.

units.title: Lydian and Lydian Dominant
units.summary: Scales with a raised 4th, for the ♯11th

cards.title: Lydian
text: Ionian (the major scale) with the 4th raised a half step is Lydian. {n:C4} Lydian contains {n:F#4}.
On maj7 chords, especially IVmaj7 or a final {c:Cmaj7}, it gives a bright, floating ♯11th sound.

cards.title: Lydian Dominant
text: Mixolydian with the 4th raised a half step is Lydian Dominant. Using {n:F#4} over {c:C7} gives a 7(♯11) sound.
It is often used on 7 chords that don't resolve, such as tritone subs or the IV7 of a blues.

cards.title: Why raise the 4th?
text: Hold {n:F4} over {c:Cmaj7} and it rubs a half step against the 3rd, {n:E4}, making a muddy sound.
Raise it a half step to {n:F#4} and the clash disappears; now it is a tension you can hold.

units.title: Quartal voicings
units.summary: Stacking 4ths instead of 3rds, the sound of modal jazz

cards.title: Stacking 4ths
text: So far, chords have been stacked in 3rds. Stack them in 4ths and you get a completely different sound.
{n:D4}, {n:G4}, {n:C5}, {n:F5}. It's unclear which note is the root, and the sound is open and floating.

cards.title: The So What voicing
text: Three perfect 4ths with a major 3rd on top: {n:E4}, {n:A4}, {n:D5}, {n:G5}, {n:B5}.
It is named after Miles Davis's "So What", where it is used as the sound of {c:Dm7} (Dorian).

cards.title: Moving along the scale
text: In modal jazz, you keep one chord and move the quartal shape in parallel along the notes of the scale.
Over {n:D4} Dorian, move the shape up one step at a time and you get a melody of chords.

units.title: Upper structure triads
units.summary: Put a triad on top of a 7 chord to sound several tensions at once

cards.title: Put a triad on top
text: The left hand (bottom) holds the root, 3rd and 7th of {c:C7}, and the right hand (top) plays a different triad.
The triad's three notes become tensions just as they are. It is much easier to grab than counting tensions one by one.
In the example, the lower three notes are {n:C4}, {n:E4}, {n:Bb4} of {c:C7}, and the upper three are a {c:D} triad ({n:D5}, {n:F#5}, {n:A5}).

cards.title: The II triad
text: Put {c:D} on top of {c:C7}: {n:D5}, {n:F#5}, {n:A5} = 9th, ♯11th, 13th.
This is the bright sound of Lydian Dominant.

cards.title: The ♭VI and VI triads
text: Put {c:Ab} on top of {c:C7} for ♭13th, root, ♯9th; put {c:A} on top for 13th, ♭9th, 3rd.
Both give an altered sound with a strong pull toward the next chord.

On the left of the example the top is an {c:Ab} triad ({n:Ab5}, {n:C6}, {n:Eb6}); on the right, an {c:A} triad ({n:A5}, {n:C#6}, {n:E6}). In both, the lower three notes are {n:C4}, {n:E4}, {n:Bb4} of {c:C7}.

units.title: Line cliché
units.summary: The chord stays the same while one voice moves by half steps

cards.title: Only one voice moves
text: {c:Dm} → {c:DmMaj7} → {c:Dm7} → {c:Dm6}.
The root {n:D5} falls by half steps, {n:C#5}, {n:C5}, {n:B4}, while the other notes stay. This is called a line cliché.

cards.title: Two new chords
text: {c:DmMaj7} (minor major seventh) is a minor triad with a major 7th on top. It sounds uneasy and cinematic.
{c:Dm6} (minor sixth) is a minor triad with a major 6th on top. It is a minor chord with Dorian brightness.

cards.title: Line clichés in tunes
text: They often appear at the start of minor-key tunes. "My Funny Valentine" is the classic example.
Even where one chord lasts a long time, a line cliché adds motion.
The example plays the same motion in {n:C4} minor: the top note falls a half step at a time, {n:C5} → {n:B4} → {n:Bb4} → {n:A4}, turning {c:Cm} into {c:CmMaj7}, {c:Cm7} and {c:Cm6}.

units.title: Melodic minor
units.summary: Dorian with a raised 7th, the jazz minor scale

cards.title: Raise the 7th a half step
text: Raise the 7th of {n:C4} Dorian ({n:C4}, {n:D4}, {n:Eb4}, {n:F4}, {n:G4}, {n:A4}, {n:Bb4}) a half step and you get {n:C4} melodic minor.
{n:C4}, {n:D4}, {n:Eb4}, {n:F4}, {n:G4}, {n:A4}, {n:B4}. It is minor, yet the upper part sounds like major.

cards.title: For m6 and m(maj7)
text: Melodic minor has a major 6th and a major 7th, so it fits {c:Cm6} and {c:CmMaj7} perfectly.
These are the two chords from the line cliché unit.

cards.title: The parent of other scales
text: Start melodic minor on its 4th note and you get Lydian Dominant; start it on its 7th note and you get Altered.
It is the source of important dominant scales used in the coming units.
The example is {c:CmMaj7}, stacking notes 1, 3, 5 and 7 of {n:C4} melodic minor. The same seven notes started on {n:F4} give {n:F4} Lydian dominant, and started on {n:B4} give {n:B4} altered.

units.title: The altered scale
units.summary: Contains ♭9th, ♯9th, ♯11th and ♭13th: the most tense scale

cards.title: Every altered note in one scale
text: The root, 3rd and 7th stay; the 9th, 13th and 5th are all shifted by a half step. By convention the ♯9th is written as the minor 3rd, {n:Eb4}.

cards.title: For 7(alt)
text: Use it when resolving to minor, like {c:C7} → {c:Fm7}, or whenever you want strong tension.
When a chart says C7alt, this is the scale to reach for.
The example adds the ♭9th {n:Db5} and ♭13th {n:Ab5} to {c:C7} and resolves to {c:Fm7}. Both notes belong to the altered scale.

cards.title: Melodic minor a half step up
text: {n:C4} Altered has the same notes as {n:Db4} melodic minor, a half step up, played from {n:C4}.
Remember it as "melodic minor a half step above the 7 chord" and you can find the notes right away.

units.title: Half-whole diminished
units.summary: An 8-note scale alternating half and whole steps

cards.title: Half, whole, repeat
text: An 8-note scale that alternates half step, whole step, half step, whole step from the root. It is also called the dominant diminished scale.

cards.title: For 7(♭9,13)
text: Along with the ♭9th and ♯9th, it also contains the natural 5th and 13th. That is the difference from Altered.
Sounding {n:A4} (13th) and {n:Db5} (♭9th) together over {c:C7} is a sound unique to this scale.

cards.title: dim7 with the gaps filled
text: Take the root out of {c:C7b9} and you get {c:Edim7}. The half-whole scale fills in one note between each note of this dim7.
Like dim7, the same shape repeats every minor 3rd, so the same notes work over four 7 chords: {n:C4}, {n:Eb4}, {n:F#4} and {n:A4}.

units.title: Whole tone
units.summary: A 6-note scale made only of whole steps, and 7(♯5)

cards.title: Six notes, all whole steps
text: {n:C4}, {n:D4}, {n:E4}, {n:F#4}, {n:G#4}, {n:Bb4}. Every step is a whole step, so six notes bring you back to the octave.
It has the same shape from any note, so it sounds dreamlike, with nowhere in particular to go.

cards.title: The 7(♯5) chord
text: {c:C7#5} is {c:C7} with the 5th raised a half step: {n:C4}, {n:E4}, {n:G#4}, {n:Bb4}.
All four notes are in the whole tone scale. That is why whole tone fits 7(♯5).

cards.title: A sound Monk loved
text: Thelonious Monk often played fast phrases running down the whole tone scale.
In {c:C7#5} → {c:Fmaj7}, the ♯5, {n:G#4}, rises a half step to {n:A4} and resolves.

units.title: Choosing a scale from tensions
units.summary: Decide the scale from the notes you want on a 7 chord

cards.title: Five dominant scales
text: Mixolydian: 9th, 13th. Lydian Dominant: 9th, ♯11th, 13th.
Half-whole diminished: ♭9th, ♯9th, 13th. Altered: ♭9th, ♯9th, ♭13th. Whole tone: 9th, ♯11th, ♯5.
The example is the base {c:C7}. Its root, 3rd and 7th ({n:C4}, {n:E4}, {n:Bb4}) are in all five scales; what differs is the tensions added on top.

cards.title: Choose by destination
text: Resolving to major, start with Mixolydian. Resolving to minor, use Altered or half-whole diminished, which contain the ♭9th and ♭13th.
For 7 chords that don't resolve (tritone subs or the IV7 of a blues), Lydian Dominant suits well.
The first half of the example resolves to major, {c:C7} → {c:Fmaj7} (Mixolydian); the second half resolves to minor, {c:C7} → {c:Fm7} (altered or half-whole).

cards.title: Reading tensions on a chart
text: C7(♭9,13) means half-whole diminished, C7(♯11) means Lydian Dominant, C7(♯5) means whole tone.
Choose a scale that contains every tension written, and you can't go wrong.
The example is {c:C7} with the ♭9th {n:Db5} and 13th {n:A5} on top. Only the half-whole scale contains both.

units.title: Avoid notes
units.summary: Scale notes that clash with the chord if you hold them

cards.title: Notes that clash a half step above
text: When you play Ionian ({n:C4}–{n:B4}) over {c:Cmaj7}, holding {n:F4} sounds muddy.
That's because {n:F4} is a half step (a minor 9th) above the chord's 3rd, {n:E4}. A note like this is called an avoid note.

cards.title: Avoid notes by chord
text: On maj7 (Ionian) and 7 (Mixolydian), the 11th (the 4th note) is the avoid note; on m7♭5 (Locrian), it's the ♭9th (the 2nd note).
m7 (Dorian) has no note that clashes a half step with a chord tone, so you can use almost every note freely.
For the three chords in the example, the avoid notes are {n:F4} over {c:Cmaj7} and {c:C7}, and {n:Db4} over {c:Cm7b5}.

cards.title: Not forbidden
text: Avoid notes work fine as short passing notes. What you avoid is holding them on a strong beat.
Lydian, which uses {n:F#4} as a ♯11th over {c:Cmaj7}, can be seen as a scale with the avoid note removed.
In the first half of the example, {n:F4} only passes briefly between {n:E4} and {n:G4}; the second half uses the ♯11th {n:F#4} instead.

units.title: Bebop scales
units.summary: 8-note scales with one passing note, putting chord tones on the beat

cards.title: Mixolydian + major 7th
text: {n:C4} bebop dominant: {n:C4}, {n:D4}, {n:E4}, {n:F4}, {n:G4}, {n:A4}, {n:Bb4}, {n:B4}.
Eight notes: Mixolydian with a passing {n:B4} added between {n:Bb4} and {n:C5}.

cards.title: Why eight notes?
text: Run down a 7-note scale in eighth notes and the chord tones drift off the beat.
With eight notes, descending from the root always puts chord tones on the beat: {n:C5}, {n:Bb4}, {n:G4}, {n:E4}. This is a secret of Charlie Parker's phrases.
The example is the chord tones that land on the beats, {n:C4}, {n:E4}, {n:G4}, {n:Bb4}, which is {c:C7} itself. Going down the previous card's example, these four come every other note.

cards.title: Bebop major
text: On major chords, add the ♯5, {n:G#4}, between Ionian's {n:G4} and {n:A4}.

units.title: Using pentatonics
units.summary: Choose tensions by which note you start a 5-note scale on

cards.title: Two pentatonics
text: Major pentatonic: {n:C4}, {n:D4}, {n:E4}, {n:G4}, {n:A4}. The major scale without its 4th and 7th notes.
Minor pentatonic: {n:C4}, {n:Eb4}, {n:F4}, {n:G4}, {n:Bb4}. The five notes everyone knows from the blues.

cards.title: Shift it for the ♯11th
text: Over {c:Cmaj7}, play the major pentatonic starting a whole step up on {n:D4} ({n:D4}, {n:E4}, {n:F#4}, {n:A4}, {n:B4}). It brings in the ♯11th, {n:F#4}, for a Lydian sound.
Keep the same 5-note shape and pick tensions just by the starting note. That's what makes pentatonics so handy.

cards.title: The tritone pentatonic for altered sounds
text: Over {c:C7}, play the major pentatonic starting a diminished 5th up on {n:Gb4} ({n:Gb4}, {n:Ab4}, {n:Bb4}, {n:Db5}, {n:Eb5}). You get the ♭9th, ♯9th, ♯11th and ♭13th.
You can get an altered sound with five notes, without learning the whole altered scale.

units.title: Slash chords
units.summary: A triad over a bass note: an easy way to write tension sounds

cards.title: Bottom is the bass, top is the triad
text: {c:Bb}/{n:C3} means the bass plays {n:C3} and a {c:Bb} triad ({n:Bb3}, {n:D4}, {n:F4}) sits on top.
From {n:C3}, these are the 7th, 9th and 11th: {c:C7sus4} without a 3rd, plus a 9th. It sounds like 9sus4.

cards.title: Four common shapes
text: Triad a minor 7th above the bass → 9sus4. A whole step above → Lydian (♯11th). A minor 3rd above → m7.
A half step above → Phrygian (sus4, ♭9th). You can hear it in tunes like Herbie Hancock's "Maiden Voyage".
The left of the example is {c:D}/{n:C3} (a whole step above: Lydian), the right is {c:Db}/{n:C3} (a half step above: Phrygian).

cards.title: Why it's handy
text: Rather than long names like 9sus4 or (♭9)sus4, writing a triad and a bass is faster to play and easier to imagine.
On piano, right hand plays the triad and left hand the bass. On sax, just line up the triad's notes and your phrase has tensions built in.
The example is the minor-third-above shape, {c:Eb}/{n:C3}: {n:C3}, {n:Eb4}, {n:G4}, {n:Bb4}, the same notes as {c:Cm7}.

units.title: Drop 2 voicings
units.summary: Drop the second note from the top an octave for a wider chord

cards.title: Close and drop 2
text: Notes stacked with no gaps, like {n:C4}, {n:E4}, {n:G4}, {n:B4}, form a close voicing.
Drop the second note from the top, {n:G4}, an octave: {n:G3}, {n:C4}, {n:E4}, {n:B4}. That is drop 2.

cards.title: Why drop it?
text: Close voicings are packed tight and sound a little muffled. Drop 2 spreads the notes for a brighter, more open sound.
It is easy to finger on guitar, and it is the most common shape for four-part sax section harmony.
The left of the example is a close {c:Dm7} ({n:F4}, {n:A4}, {n:C5}, {n:E5}); the right drops the second note from the top, {n:C5}, an octave to make drop 2 ({n:C4}, {n:F4}, {n:A4}, {n:E5}).

cards.title: Works on inversions too
text: For the inversion {n:E4}, {n:G4}, {n:B4}, {n:C5}, drop the second from the top, {n:B4}: {n:B3}, {n:E4}, {n:G4}, {n:C5}.
Each of the four inversions has its own drop 2, so you can choose the top note to match the melody.

units.title: Harmonic minor
units.summary: The scale behind V7 in a minor key, and Phrygian Dominant

cards.title: Raise only the 7th
text: {n:C4} harmonic minor: {n:C4}, {n:D4}, {n:Eb4}, {n:F4}, {n:G4}, {n:Ab4}, {n:B4}.
Natural minor with the 7th raised a half step. The gap of a step and a half between {n:Ab4} and {n:B4} gives it a Middle Eastern flavor.

cards.title: Where the minor key's V7 comes from
text: In natural minor, the chord on the 5th note is {c:Gm7}. Raising the 7th to {n:B4} turns it into {c:G7}, which resolves strongly to {c:Cm7}.
The minor II–V uses {c:G7b9} because its ♭9th, {n:Ab4}, is also in this scale.
The example ends on {c:CmMaj7} rather than {c:Cm7} because the 7th of this scale is {n:B4}, so stacking on {n:C4} gives a major 7th.

cards.title: Phrygian Dominant
text: Play {n:C4} harmonic minor from its 5th note, {n:G4}: {n:G4}, {n:Ab4}, {n:B4}, {n:C5}, {n:D5}, {n:Eb5}, {n:F5}. This is called Phrygian Dominant.
It contains the ♭9th and ♭13th, so it is perfect for {c:G7b9} resolving to minor.

units.title: The diminished scale
units.summary: Whole and half steps in turn: a scale for dim7

cards.title: Start with a whole step
text: Eight notes going whole, half, whole, half... It is the reverse order of the half-whole diminished scale (which starts with a half step).

cards.title: Add a whole step above each dim7 note
text: Add {n:E4}, {n:G4}, {n:Bb4}, {n:C#5}, a whole step above each note of {c:Ddim7} ({n:D4}, {n:F4}, {n:Ab4}, {n:Cb5}), and you get this scale.
The four added notes form another dim7. The scale combines two dim7 chords.

cards.title: When to use which
text: dim7 chords take the diminished scale starting with a whole step; 7(♭9) chords take the half-whole scale starting with a half step.
The same eight notes play a different role depending on where you start counting.

The two chords in the example can actually be played with the same eight notes: whether you start on {n:D4} with a whole step or on {n:G4} with a half step, you use {n:D4}, {n:E4}, {n:F4}, {n:G4}, {n:Ab4}, {n:Bb4}, {n:B4}, {n:C#5}.

units.title: The So What voicing
units.summary: Three 4ths and a major 3rd: the sound of modal jazz

cards.title: Modal jazz
text: From the late 1950s, a style emerged that stays on one scale (mode) for a long time instead of changing chords quickly. This is called modal jazz.
For example, 16 bars of {c:Dm7} Dorian, then a move straight up a half step to {c:Ebm7}.

cards.title: Three 4ths, then a major 3rd
text: {n:D4}, {n:G4}, {n:C5}, {n:F5}, {n:A5}. Three perfect 4ths stacked, with only the top interval a major 3rd.
It is the sound pianist Bill Evans used, and it is called the So What voicing after the tune.

cards.title: Move it in parallel along the scale
text: Move the same shape up and down over Dorian notes and you get a floating, modal-jazz accompaniment.
The major 3rd on top adds a minor color to the quartal sound from the earlier unit.
The right of the example shifts the same shape up one Dorian step ({n:E4}, {n:A4}, {n:D5}, {n:G5}, {n:B5}).

units.title: Side-slipping
units.summary: Step out a half step on purpose, then return to release the tension

cards.title: Shift a half step
text: While playing Dorian over {c:Dm7}, move to the Dorian of {c:Ebm7}, a half step up.
Most notes now clash with the chord, creating strong tension. This is called side-slipping.

cards.title: Always come back
text: When you return to the original scale, the tension releases and listeners hear that you stepped out on purpose.
If you stay out, it just sounds like a mistake. The trick is to step out briefly and come right back.

cards.title: Effective in modal jazz
text: In modal jazz, where one chord lasts a long time, this kind of stepping out keeps things from getting monotonous.
John Coltrane and McCoy Tyner were masters of it. You can also slip a half step down.
The example slips from {c:Dm7} to {c:Ebm7} a half step up, then comes back to {c:Dm7}.

units.title: Reharmonization
units.summary: Put different chords under the same melody with the tools so far

cards.title: Rewriting the chords
text: Keeping the melody and changing only the chords is called reharmonization (reharm).
It is a basic arranging skill for making a standard your own.
The example is the original progression before reharmonizing, a two-five-one. The next card rewrites it with different tools.

cards.title: Four tools
text: Tritone sub: {c:G7}→{c:Db7}. Secondary dominant: {c:Am7}→{c:A7}.
Passing diminished: {c:C#dim7} between {c:Cmaj7} and {c:Dm7}. Backdoor: {c:Fm7} → {c:Bb7} instead of {c:Dm7} → {c:G7}.
The example uses the first tool, the tritone sub: {c:G7} is replaced by {c:Db7}.

cards.title: Check the melody notes
text: Always check that the new chord doesn't clash with the melody. If the melody note is a chord tone or a tension, you're fine.
For example, if the melody is {n:F4}, it works as the 7th of {c:G7} and the 3rd of {c:Db7}, so the tritone sub is safe.

units.title: Rootless voicings
units.summary: Piano comping with 3rds, 7ths and tensions, leaving the root to the bass

cards.title: Leave out the root
text: In a band the bass plays the root, so the pianist leaves it out and comps with four notes: the 3rd and 7th plus tensions. This is called a rootless voicing.
For {c:Dm7}: {n:F4}, {n:A4}, {n:C5}, {n:E5}. The 9th, {n:E5}, takes the place of the root, {n:D4}.

cards.title: Type A and type B
text: Type A stacks from the 3rd (3-5-7-9); type B stacks from the 7th (7-9-3-5).
On 7 chords, the 13th usually replaces the 5th. Type B for {c:G7} is {n:F4}, {n:A4}, {n:B4}, {n:E5}.
The example compares them on {c:Cmaj7}: the left is type A ({n:E4}, {n:G4}, {n:B4}, {n:D5} = 3-5-7-9), the right is type B ({n:B3}, {n:D4}, {n:E4}, {n:G4} = 7-9-3-5).

cards.title: Alternate on a II–V
text: Play {c:Dm7} as type A and {c:G7} as type B, and only one note moves: {n:C5}→{n:B4}.
Alternate IIm7 type A → V7 type B → Imaj7 type A and the chords connect smoothly with almost no hand movement.

units.title: Triad pairs
units.summary: Alternate two triads with no shared notes to make a 6-note scale

cards.title: Two triads
text: {c:F} ({n:F4}, {n:A4}, {n:C5}) and {c:G} ({n:G4}, {n:B4}, {n:D5}) share no notes.
Alternate them and you get six notes that sound like a single scale. This is called a triad pair.

cards.title: Choose them to fit the chord
text: For {c:Dm7} (Dorian), {c:F} and {c:G} on the 3rd and 4th. For {c:Cmaj7} (Lydian), {c:C} and {c:D} on the root and a whole step up.
For {c:G7} (Altered), {c:Db} and {c:Eb} on the diminished 5th and minor 6th.
The example is the {c:Db} / {c:Eb} pair over {c:G7}. Its six notes, {n:Db4}, {n:F4}, {n:Ab4}, {n:Eb4}, {n:G4}, {n:Bb4}, all belong to {n:G4} altered.

cards.title: Wide intervals
text: Unlike running up a scale, triads leap in 3rds and 4ths, which gives wide, modern-sounding phrases.
Saxophonists George Garzone and Kenny Garrett use this approach a lot.

units.title: Enclosures
units.summary: A bebop technique that surrounds a target note from above and below

cards.title: Surround it from above and below
text: To target the 3rd of {c:Cmaj7}, {n:E4}, don't play it right away. Play {n:F4} above and {n:D#4} below first, then land on {n:E4}.
Because it surrounds (encloses) the target note, it is called an enclosure.

cards.title: Scale note above, half step below
text: The usual rule: the note above is the neighboring scale note, and the note below is a half step under. The lower note may be outside the scale.
The outside note sounds for just a moment and resolves at once, so the landing note comes through clearly.
The example targets {n:D5}, the 5th of {c:G7}: above is the scale neighbor {n:E5}, below is {n:C#5} a half step under, a note outside the key.

cards.title: Land on a strong beat
text: Put the two surrounding notes on weak beats and the target on a strong beat, like the downbeat, and the chord tone comes through clearly.
It is a basic bebop phrase that shows up countless times in Charlie Parker's lines.

units.title: Modal interchange
units.summary: Borrow chords from the parallel minor to cast a shadow over a tune

cards.title: Borrowing from the parallel minor
text: In a {n:C4} major tune, briefly borrowing diatonic chords from {n:C4} minor is called modal interchange.
The subdominant minor {c:Fm7} is actually one of these borrowed chords.

cards.title: Commonly borrowed chords
text: ♭IIImaj7 ({c:Ebmaj7}), IVm7 ({c:Fm7}), ♭VImaj7 ({c:Abmaj7}), ♭VII7 ({c:Bb7}), IIm7♭5 ({c:Dm7b5}).
All of them contain minor-key notes such as {n:Eb4}, {n:Ab4} and {n:Bb4}.

cards.title: A shadow in the brightness
text: Go {c:Cmaj7} → {c:Abmaj7} → {c:Cmaj7} and the sound changes for a moment, as if a cloud passed over.
It is a color often used at the end of ballads or just before the chorus.

units.title: Block chords
units.summary: Pack chord tones under the melody and play it as solid chords

cards.title: Pack them under the melody
text: Under each melody note, line up the rest of the chord with no gaps and move it as a solid block. This is called block chords.
With melody {n:E5} on {c:Cmaj7}, put {n:C5}, {n:B4}, {n:G4} underneath.

cards.title: Double the melody at the bottom
text: Then the left hand adds {n:E4}, an octave below the melody, so the melody sounds in two voices.
The melody stands out thick and strong, which is why it is also called locked hands.

cards.title: From piano to big band
text: Pianists George Shearing and Red Garland made this sound popular.
A big band sax "soli", with five players moving in the same shape, is built on the same idea.
The example uses the same shape twice: {c:Cmaj7} packed under the melody {n:E5}, then {c:Dm7} under the melody {n:D5}, each doubling the melody at the bottom.

units.title: Pedal point
units.summary: Hold a low note while only the chords above it move

cards.title: Keep holding a low note
text: The bass holds the same note while the chords above it change. This is called a pedal point, named after the organ's foot keyboard (pedals).
Hold {n:C3} under {c:Cmaj7} → {c:Dm7} → {c:Cmaj7}. The unmoving bass gives the sound stability.

cards.title: Dominant pedal
text: Holding the 5th of the key, {n:G3} in {n:C4}, is a dominant pedal.
Even if {c:Dm7} or {c:Fmaj7} is played above, the bass stays on the root of {c:G7}, so the tension of waiting to resolve to {c:Cmaj7} goes on.
In the example the bass holds {n:G3} through {c:Dm7} → {c:G7}, and finally the bass moves to {n:C4} as it resolves to {c:Cmaj7}.

cards.title: In intros and endings
text: It is often used in intros, endings and climaxes of solos.
A tonic pedal feels settled; a dominant pedal builds the expectation that something is coming.
The example plays {c:Dm7} → {c:G7} → {c:Cmaj7} without a pedal. Compare it with the previous card to hear the tension a held bass adds.

units.title: Constant structure
units.summary: Move the same chord type in parallel, free of the key

cards.title: Move the same shape
text: {c:Ebmaj7} → {c:Cmaj7} → {c:Amaj7}. All stay maj7, falling a minor 3rd each time.
Moving the same type of chord in a row is called constant structure.

cards.title: Free from the rules of the key
text: The next chord is decided by how far you move, not by diatonic chords or II–V rules.
It is a new 1960s sound heard in Herbie Hancock's "Dolphin Dance" and Joe Henderson's "Inner Urge".
The example is {c:Dm7} → {c:Cm7} → {c:Bbm7}: the m7 shape steps down a whole step each time, a motion no two-five rule explains.

cards.title: Share the melody note
text: Even if the distances vary, choosing chords so the melody note is always one of the chord tones makes them connect naturally.
Under melody {n:G4}: {c:Ebmaj7} (3rd) → {c:Cmaj7} (5th) → {c:Abmaj7} (7th).

units.title: Digital patterns
units.summary: 4-note shapes like 1-2-3-5 that spell out the chord clearly

text: Over {c:Cmaj7}: {n:C4}, {n:D4}, {n:E4}, {n:G4}. Four notes: root, 2nd, 3rd, 5th.
They are called digital patterns because they can be written as numbers. Four notes fill two beats, so they fit neatly into chord changes.

cards.title: Apply it to each chord
text: In tunes with fast-moving chords like "Giant Steps", John Coltrane applied 1-2-3-5 to each chord.
For {c:Dm7}: {n:D4}, {n:E4}, {n:F4}, {n:A4}. On a minor chord the 3rd becomes a minor 3rd.

cards.title: Vary the shape
text: Combine it with 1-3-5-7 (the chord tones themselves), 3-5-7-9 (up from the 3rd), the reversed 5-3-2-1, and so on.
3-5-7-9 reaches the 9th tension without playing the root, so it sounds modern.

units.title: Negative harmony
units.summary: Mirror chords across the key's axis to make darker substitutes

cards.title: Reflect it in a mirror
text: In the key of {n:C4}, notes are flipped around the axis exactly halfway between {n:C4} and {n:G4} (between {n:Eb4} and {n:E4}).
{n:C4}↔{n:G4}, {n:D4}↔{n:F4}, {n:E4}↔{n:Eb4}, {n:A4}↔{n:Bb4}, {n:B4}↔{n:Ab4}. Bright notes swap for dark ones.

cards.title: V7 becomes IIm7♭5
text: Mirror the four notes of {c:G7} and, reordered from the bottom, they become {c:Dm7b5}.
It belongs to the subdominant minor family, so it can resolve to {c:Cmaj7} in place of {c:G7}.

cards.title: Mirroring a II–V
text: Mirror {c:Dm7} → {c:G7} and you get {c:Gm7} → {c:Dm7b5}. Then go back to {c:Cmaj7} at the end.
Popularized by musician Jacob Collier, it lets you create modal-interchange-like shadows by a fixed rule.

units.title: Pivot chord modulation
units.summary: Use a chord shared by two keys as a stepping stone to a new key

cards.title: Chords in both keys
text: Compare the diatonic chords of {n:C4} and {n:G4}: {c:Cmaj7}, {c:Em7} and {c:Am7} appear in both.
A shared chord like this is called a pivot chord.

cards.title: Reinterpret its role
text: {c:Am7} is VIm7 in {n:C4} and IIm7 in {n:G4}.
Go {c:Cmaj7} → {c:Am7}, hear {c:Am7} as IIm7, then continue {c:D7} → {c:Gmaj7}, and you move naturally to the key of {n:G4}.

cards.title: Confirm the new key with V7
text: Sounding the new key's V7 after the pivot chord makes the modulation clear.
It is the smoothest kind of modulation, often used when a standard's bridge moves to another key.
In the example, after {c:Fmaj7} (IVmaj7 in {n:C4}), {c:Em7}, found in both keys, is reread as IIm7 of {n:D4}; {c:A7} confirms the key of {n:D4} and leads to {c:Dmaj7}.

units.title: In a tune: the Autumn Leaves pattern
units.summary: Apply the techniques to 8 bars of major and minor II–Vs

cards.title: The shape of the progression
text: The same shape as the opening of the standard "Autumn Leaves". A II–V–I in {n:G4} is followed by a II–V–I in {n:E4} minor.
The example plays the first four ({c:Am7} → {c:D7} → {c:Gmaj7} → {c:Cmaj7}).

cards.title: Add tritone subs
text: {c:D7} falls a 5th to the next chord, {c:Gmaj7}, so it can be replaced by its tritone sub, {c:Ab7}.
Replace {c:B7} with {c:F7} too, and the bass walks down a half step to {c:Em6}.

cards.title: Come home by the backdoor
text: Rewrite {c:Am7} → {c:D7} → {c:Gmaj7} as {c:Cm7} → {c:F7} → {c:Gmaj7}.
It returns to the tonic by another road, through the shadow of IVm7 → ♭VII7.

cards.title: Scales and guide tones
text: On the major side, {c:Am7} takes Dorian and {c:Cmaj7} takes Lydian. On the minor side, {c:B7} takes Phrygian Dominant and {c:Em6} takes melodic minor.
Play a line where each 7th falls a half or whole step to the next chord's 3rd, and the moment the chord changes comes through clearly.
The example is the minor side, {c:F#m7b5} → {c:B7} → {c:Em6}.

units.title: In a tune: rhythm changes
units.summary: Use secondary dominants and tritone subs on I-VI-II-V and the bridge's chain of dominants

cards.title: The A section
text: {c:Bbmaj7} → {c:Gm7} → {c:Cm7} → {c:F7}, repeated: the I-VI-II-V turnaround.
It is the shape of Gershwin's "I Got Rhythm", so it is called rhythm changes.

cards.title: VIm7 into VI7
text: Turn {c:Gm7} into {c:G7} and it becomes a secondary dominant heading to {c:Cm7}.
It resolves to a minor chord, so Phrygian Dominant fits.

cards.title: The bridge is a chain of dominants
text: {c:D7} → {c:G7} → {c:C7} → {c:F7}. Each is a 7 chord falling a 5th to the next.
Each can be replaced by its tritone sub: {c:Ab7}, {c:Db7}, {c:Gb7}, {c:B7}.

cards.title: Read by role
text: Learn chords by role (Imaj7, VI7, IIm7 and so on) rather than by name, and you can apply the same techniques in any key.
Make {c:F7} its tritone sub, {c:B7}, and the bass walks down by half steps: {c:Cm7} → {c:B7} → {c:Bbmaj7}.

units.title: In a tune: minor blues
units.summary: Choose scales and guide tones over 12 bars built on Im7 and IVm7

cards.title: The 12-bar form
text: {c:Cm7} for 4 bars, {c:Fm7} for 2 bars, {c:Cm7} for 2 bars. The last 4 bars are {c:Ab7} → {c:G7} → {c:Cm7} → {c:G7}.
The example lists each chord once, in the order they appear: {c:Cm7}, {c:Fm7}, {c:Ab7}, {c:G7}.

cards.title: From ♭VI7 to V7
text: {c:Ab7} is a half step above {c:G7}. It works like the tritone sub of {c:D7}, with the bass walking down a half step.
Lydian Dominant, with its ♯11th, fits well.

cards.title: V7 takes Phrygian Dominant
text: {c:G7} resolves to the minor {c:Cm7}, so Phrygian Dominant, with its ♭9th and ♭13th, fits.

cards.title: Im7 and IVm7 take Dorian
text: Both {c:Cm7} and {c:Fm7} can be played with Dorian.
The 7th of {c:Cm7}, {n:Bb4}, falls a whole step to the 3rd of {c:Fm7}, {n:Ab4}.
